title: Linear Dependence
body:
A set of [[Vector|vectors]] is **linearly dependent** when one of them is redundant: it can be
written as a linear combination of the others, so removing it does not shrink the
[[Vector Space|span]]. If none of them is redundant, the set is **linearly independent**.

## The definition you actually use

$\{\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_k\}$ is linearly **independent** when

$$
c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2\mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + c_k\mathbf{v}_k = \mathbf{0}
\quad\text{forces}\quad c_1 = c_2 = \cdots = c_k = 0
$$

and **dependent** when some combination with at least one $c_i \neq 0$ gives $\mathbf{0}$.

The two phrasings agree: if $c_1 \neq 0$ you can divide through and solve for $\mathbf{v}_1$ in
terms of the rest, which is the redundancy. The zero-combination version is the one to work
with, because it is a computation rather than a search.

## Testing it

Stack the vectors as the **columns** of a [[Matrix]] $A$. Then the definition is exactly the
homogeneous system $A\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{0}$, and you already know how to solve those:

- run [[Gaussian Elimination]] to echelon form
- **a pivot in every column** means only the trivial solution, so **independent**
- **any free variable** means non-trivial solutions exist, so **dependent**, and the free
  variable tells you which vector to blame

For $k$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^k$ (a square $A$) there is a shortcut: independent exactly when
$\det A \neq 0$. Which is the same statement as $A$ being invertible, as the columns forming a
[[Basis]], and as every other row of the equivalence table in [[Matrix Inverse]]. That table is
where these threads join.

Example:

$$
\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}, \;
\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix}3\\6\end{bmatrix}
\qquad
3\mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{0}
$$

Dependent, and visibly so: $\mathbf{v}_2$ is $3\mathbf{v}_1$, the same direction, spanning the
same line. Two vectors are dependent exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other, which
makes the $k=2$ case checkable by eye. **This shortcut does not extend to three or more**: three
vectors can be pairwise non-parallel and still dependent, if they happen to lie in a common
plane.

## Facts worth knowing cold

- **More than $n$ vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are always dependent.** You cannot fit five
  independent directions in four-dimensional space. This is the counting argument behind
  "dimension is well defined" in [[Basis]].
- **Any set containing $\mathbf{0}$ is dependent**, since $1 \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}$ is a
  non-trivial combination.
- **A subset of an independent set is independent**; a superset of a dependent set is dependent.
- **Independence is about the set, not any one vector.** "This vector is dependent" is not a
  statement. Dependence is a relationship.
- Independent vectors can still span less than the whole space. Two independent vectors in
  $\mathbb{R}^3$ span a plane and nothing more. **Independence and spanning are separate
  conditions, and a [[Basis]] is what you call a set that satisfies both.**

## Why it matters

Dependence is redundancy, and redundancy in a data matrix means columns that carry no
information the others do not. Detecting and removing it is dimensionality reduction, which is
what [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE|MATH 2303]] builds
[[Principal Component Analysis|PCA]] out of. Independence is also the condition for a set of
solutions to a
[[Differential Equations|differential equation]] to be a genuine general solution rather than one
solution written twice.
